column3: The Hebrew repeats Ziklag three times and uses the collective singular Amalekite; BSB names Ziklag twice and uses plural “Amalekites.”
The Hebrew names “the women who were in it, from small to great”; BSB adds “and all who were there” and renders the size pair as “both young and old.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the accompanying group “the people” and uses singular “their voice”; BSB has “the troops” and plural “their voices.”
The Hebrew calls Abigail “Nabal’s wife”; BSB specifies “the widow of Nabal.”
The Hebrew says the people’s soul was “bitter”; BSB says each man’s soul “grieved.”
The Hebrew repeats both the ephod and David in the final bringing; BSB replaces both with pronouns. It also has a request particle in David’s instruction.

The Hebrew names the raiding band collectively in the singular; BSB uses plural “raiders.” Both overtaking and rescuing have emphatic root repetition; BSB supplies “the captives” as the object of rescue.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew states David’s pursuit before the two hundred men remaining; BSB puts their exhaustion first. The Hebrew repeats the name Besor, where BSB uses “the brook.”
The Hebrew leaves the finders unnamed and says they gave him bread and he ate, then gave him water. BSB supplies “his men,” reverses the order of food and water, and renders bread as “food.”
The Hebrew says his spirit returned to him; BSB renders this as “was revived.” It calls the food he lacked “bread.”
The Hebrew explicitly calls him an Egyptian young man; BSB leaves his youth implicit.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew twice says to lead him “down” to the raiding band; BSB leaves both downward directions implicit.
The Hebrew leaves both the man led and the raiders unnamed; BSB supplies David and “the Amalekites.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew separately says David rescued everything and rescued his two wives, repeating his name and the rescue verb. BSB combines the wives into the first recovery statement.
The Hebrew has plural “sons and daughters” and leaves the plunder-takers unnamed; BSB uses singular “son or daughter” and supplies “the Amalekites.”
The Hebrew names David as the one taking the livestock and leaves its drivers unnamed; BSB uses “he” for David and supplies “his men” as drivers.
The Hebrew repeats David’s name four times and explicitly says the exhausted men had been made to stay at Besor. BSB names him twice and leaves the causation of staying implicit.
The Hebrew quotes singular “they did not go with me”; BSB uses plural “with us.”
The Hebrew uses singular “our hand”; BSB uses plural “our hands.”
The Hebrew describes one going “down” to battle and one sitting with the equipment; BSB leaves the downward direction implicit and says “stayed with the supplies.”
The Hebrew leaves the lawgiver unnamed; BSB supplies David.
The Hebrew calls the gift “a blessing” and uses singular “his friend” collectively; BSB has “a gift” and plural “his friends.”
The Hebrew continues the recipient list without repeating a sending verb or gift noun; BSB supplies “He sent gifts.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats “cities” for the Kenite and uses collective singular ethnic names; BSB combines the two groups under one “cities” and uses plural ethnic names.
Close to the Hebrew.
